First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{4x} & ={3}^{1-x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{4x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{1-x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)=(1-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =(1-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ 4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ 4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x(4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}\end{aligned}
$$
